title: Estate and Beneficiary Basics
subtitle: Leave clear instructions, not a scavenger hunt

blocks.text: An estate plan is the paperwork that lets other people act for you when you can’t: while you’re alive but unable to manage, and after you’re gone. It isn’t about controlling every last detail. It’s about cutting confusion, delay, arguments and needless cost for whoever is left holding the job.
Paperwork has terrible timing. It shows up just when nobody wants to deal with it. A clear plan means your family spends less time hunting for account numbers and more time on what matters.

This topic deserves care, so we’ll keep the language plain. Estate law is set by each province and territory, and your own situation can change the outcome. Treat this as a starting point, and use a lawyer or notary where you live for personal advice and documents.

items.title: “A will keeps my estate out of probate entirely.”
items.text: A will sets out your wishes and names who will carry them out, but it doesn’t promise a court will skip its approval step. Probate can still apply, depending on the property, the bank and where you live.

blocks.text: Spare the people you love a paperwork mess at the hardest time of their lives.
blocks.detail: A few documents that agree with each other can save your family months of delay, cost and conflict.
blocks.extra: Section 04 shows the account forms that a will can’t reach.

sections.title: Treat Your Estate Plan Like a System

blocks.text: A will matters, but it’s one piece of a bigger machine. A complete basic plan is nine smaller jobs working together.

items.title: A valid will, made and signed under the law where you live.
An estate representative: an executor, estate trustee, personal representative or, in Quebec, a liquidator.
Incapacity documents that work while you’re still alive.
Beneficiary or successor instructions, kept up to date on every account that allows them.
A plain-language list of what you own and what you owe.
Insurance and pension information in one place.
A guardianship plan if you have children under 18.
Instructions for digital accounts and important personal property.
A safe place the right people can find.

blocks.text: Each piece works on a different timeline. A will takes effect after death. A power of attorney, whatever your province calls it, works while you’re alive, under its own rules, and ends the moment you die. From there, the estate representative takes over.
Naming the same trusted person for every role isn’t always simplest. Money decisions, health decisions, child care and running an estate each call for different skills.

The plan should also note what skips the estate altogether. Joint ownership, insurance, pensions, trusts and valid beneficiary forms can all pass property in a different way. The details depend on the asset, the contract and your province.

items.title: “Adding my adult kid as joint owner is basically the same as estate planning.”
items.text: Joint ownership can bring its own tax, creditor, control and family problems. What it does often depends on why it was set up and on your province’s law. Get advice before you change who owns something.

sections.title: The Will, and the Person Who Carries It Out

items.title: WHAT A WILL CAN DO
items.text: A will can say who gets what, name the person who runs the estate, set up trusts and give instructions for beneficiaries under 18. It can also share your wishes about who should raise your children, though a court usually has the final say.

items.title: WHAT A WILL DOESN'T CONTROL
items.text: Insurance policies, pensions, registered accounts and other contracts can name their own beneficiaries and send money around the estate. Property owned jointly can follow its own path too. A will doesn’t reach everything.

blocks.text: If you die without a valid will, called “dying intestate,” provincial or territorial law decides who runs the estate and how it’s split. Those default rules don’t know your real relationships. An unmarried partner, a stepchild, a close friend or a favourite charity can end up with nothing unless a valid document says otherwise.

items.title: “The oldest child should automatically be the executor.”
items.text: Age isn’t a job qualification. Choose based on ability, time, trust, where the person lives and how the family gets along.

blocks.text: The person who settles an estate goes by different names: executor, estate trustee, administrator or, in Quebec, liquidator. The job means finding the will, tracking down property and debts, protecting assets, telling banks and agencies, filing tax returns, paying real debts, keeping records, talking with beneficiaries and handing out what’s left. It can take a year or more.

Look for someone organized, trustworthy, willing to ask for professional help and able to handle conflict. Talk to them before you name them, and name a backup in case your first choice can’t do it. Being great at family dinners isn’t proof of being great at estate paperwork, so use the real job description.
An executor can also be a beneficiary. That’s fine, but they must keep their own interest separate from their duties, with careful records.

sections.title: Give Beneficiary Designations Their Own Review

blocks.text: A beneficiary is whoever is meant to receive the money or property. A beneficiary isn’t automatically the executor, and an executor isn’t automatically an heir. Beneficiary instructions can sit on life insurance, TFSAs, RRSPs, RRIFs, pensions and annuities, and what they do depends on the plan and your province. Trust the record the institution has on file, not a note in a personal folder.

items.title: TFSA: SUCCESSOR HOLDER VS. BENEFICIARY
items.text: Where it’s allowed, a spouse or common-law partner can be named successor holder. They take over the account, and the TFSA keeps its tax-free status. A beneficiary gets the money instead of the account, and growth after death can be taxed. In Quebec, you can’t name a successor holder or beneficiary on the TFSA form itself, so it has to be done in your will.

items.title: RRSP AND RRIF DESIGNATIONS
items.text: Under the usual rule, the full value of an RRSP or RRIF is added to the person’s income in the year they die. A tax-free rollover may be possible to a spouse or common-law partner, or to a financially dependent child or grandchild, but the conditions, forms and deadlines matter. Naming a beneficiary doesn’t make that tax disappear. The person who gets the account and the estate that pays the tax may not be the same.

items.title: PENSIONS AND LIFE INSURANCE
items.text: Workplace pensions can include survivor benefits under their own rules. A form signed years ago might not reflect a relationship that has since changed. Life insurance can have both a first and a backup beneficiary. Ask the insurer or plan administrator to confirm, in writing, what’s on file.

blocks.text: A new will, a wedding or a divorce doesn’t change your account forms on its own. Check each one after any big life event.

items.title: “A new will automatically updates every account.”
items.text: Account contracts and beneficiary forms can run on their own track, separate from the will. Review both together, account by account.

blocks.text: Priya makes the records agree
paragraphs: Priya, 58, lived in Kamloops. She owned her home, had a workplace pension, an RRSP, two TFSAs at different banks and a life insurance policy. Her will named her sister Meena as executor and split everything between her two adult children, Arjun and Lena.

One January, after a friend’s family spent months untangling an estate, Priya decided to check her own. She called each bank and the insurer and asked them to confirm, in writing, who was named on each account.

The answers stopped her cold. One TFSA still named her former partner, from a relationship that ended twelve years earlier. Her pension had no survivor contact at all. And the life insurance named only Lena, because Arjun hadn’t been born when she signed the form.

Her first impulse was to log in that night and change everything online. Then she paused. A quick fix might clash with her will, or with the tax on her RRSP. She booked an estate lawyer and an accountant instead, and brought her statements, her will and a list of what she wanted for her children.

They showed her which forms she could update directly and which wishes belonged in her will. The accountant pointed out a surprise: if her RRSP went straight to Lena, the estate would still owe the tax on it, which would shrink Arjun’s share. Priya rebalanced her plan so both children would end up treated fairly.

Then she called Meena, named a backup executor and built a short estate file. She gave her children something more useful than balances or passwords: who to call, and where the plan lives. She set a reminder to check the forms every January, the same week she renews her car insurance.

blocks.text: One yearly check can catch the mistakes that would cost your family the most.
blocks.detail: Making your will and your account forms agree, while you still can, turns good intentions into a plan that works.
blocks.extra: Section 07 shows how to build your own estate file.

sections.title: Plan for Incapacity, Not Just Death

blocks.text: People often think about estate plans after a health scare. Incapacity papers solve a different problem: they let someone make set choices for you while you’re alive but can’t make them yourself.

The names change across the country. The money version may be called a power of attorney for property, an enduring power of attorney or a mandate. The health version may be called a personal directive, a power of attorney for personal care or an advance directive.

A basic power of attorney can stop working the moment someone loses mental capacity. An enduring or continuing version is built to keep working through incapacity, if it meets your province’s rules. Don’t trust a downloaded form just because of its title. Check what it does, when it starts and whether it lasts through incapacity where you live.

Choose decision-makers with the same care you’d use for an executor. Whoever handles money should understand record-keeping and conflicts of interest. Whoever handles health or personal care should know your values and be able to speak up under pressure. Talk to them before you sign, give them what they need to act and keep sensitive records protected.
A power of attorney ends at death. It doesn’t let anyone keep paying bills or handing out property as if they were the executor.
An estate file is a map, not a vault for every secret. It tells your representative what exists, where the real records are and who to call.

items.title: IDENTITY & LEGAL DOCUMENTS
items.text: Your full legal name, province or territory, marital status and key contacts. Note where the original will and incapacity documents are, plus your lawyer’s or notary’s contact details. Don’t leave the only original will somewhere nobody can reach. A safe deposit box can be hard to open quickly.

items.title: ASSETS & DEBTS
items.text: Banks, account types, the last four digits of account numbers, property addresses, pensions, insurance policies, business interests, loans, credit cards and anything valuable. Update it whenever an account opens, closes or moves.

items.title: DIGITAL & PASSWORDS
items.text: Don’t write full passwords into the list. Use a trusted password manager with emergency access, or leave instructions your lawyer has approved. Note how to find online businesses, websites, subscriptions, loyalty points, cloud storage, crypto and social media accounts.

items.title: TAX & GOVERNMENT INFO
items.text: Your representative will likely need past tax returns, notices of assessment, property records, benefit details and your SIN. The CRA won’t share tax records without proof. That usually means a death certificate and the paper that names the executor or liquidator.

blocks.text: The representative must also file a final tax return for the year of death. It’s due April 30 of the next year, or six months after death if the person died in November or December. They may also need a T3 return for the estate and a CRA clearance certificate before handing anything out. Giving out property while tax is still owing can make them personally responsible, up to the amount they gave out.

At death, the tax rules treat most investments and property as if they were sold that day, so any gain is taxed on the final return. Property left to a spouse or common-law partner can usually roll over without tax until they sell or die, and your main home is generally covered by the principal residence exemption. A tax professional can show what your estate may owe, so you can plan for it.

Add practical notes too: pets, personal items, funeral wishes, gifts to charity and who should be told. These aren’t legally binding on their own, but they help your representative guess less. Keep them consistent with the will.
Tell your executor where the actual will is stored. Taping the only clue to the back of the will itself is a filing system designed by a mystery novelist.

sections.title: What Changes by Province or Territory

blocks.text: Most estate law is set by each province or territory. The same paper can work in a different way, depending on where you live.

items.title: How a will must be signed and witnessed
items.text: The rules are different in each province or territory.

items.title: Whether electronic wills are allowed
items.text: Not every province recognizes a digital will.

items.title: The name and authority of the estate representative
items.text: Executor, estate trustee, administrator or liquidator, depending on where you live.

items.title: Rights of spouses, partners, dependants and children
items.text: Some family members can have legal claims, whatever the will says.

items.title: What happens without a valid will
items.text: The default rules may not match your real relationships.

items.title: Probate or estate administration procedures
items.text: Court steps and fees vary. Ontario, for example, charges $15 for every $1,000 of estate value above $50,000.

items.title: Rules for beneficiary designations and joint property
items.text: What passes outside the will differs from province to province.

items.title: Documents used during incapacity
items.text: Money and health decision forms have different names and rules.

items.title: Family claims that can change a distribution
items.text: Some claims can override what the will or default rules say.

blocks.text: Ontario tends to use “estate trustee” and “continuing power of attorney.” British Columbia follows its Wills, Estates and Succession Act, accepts electronic wills and has a Wills Registry where you can record where your will is kept. Quebec follows civil law and uses the words “succession” and “liquidator.” It accepts notarial wills, wills signed before witnesses and handwritten wills, each with its own rules. A Quebec will that isn’t notarial generally needs to be verified after death, and a notarial one doesn’t.

These are examples, not a full guide. Use your province’s free legal help line or website, and have your papers checked where you live. Moving provinces, marrying, separating, divorcing, having a child, starting a business or buying property outside Canada are all good reasons for a fresh look.
Key takeaway

A basic estate plan is a set of papers that agree with each other: the will, the people you’ve named, the account forms, the health and money papers, the tax plan and the estate file. Clear documents matter, but organized information is what makes them usable.

Run a one-page check: write the names on your will, then on every insurance policy, registered account, pension and incapacity document. Flag anything that doesn’t match. Leave account values off this page.

items.title: When does a power of attorney's authority end?
items.detail: At death. What it can do while you’re alive depends on the document and your province’s rules.

items.title: What’s the difference between an executor and a beneficiary?
items.detail: The executor runs the estate. A beneficiary receives money or property from it.

items.title: Why treat a TFSA successor holder differently from a TFSA beneficiary?
items.detail: Where allowed, a successor holder takes over the account itself. A beneficiary receives the money instead, under different tax and account rules.

items.title: Give two reasons to review an account designation alongside the will.
items.detail: A beneficiary form can send money around the estate entirely, and the person who gets the account may not be the one whose estate pays the tax on it. Old forms can also clash with what you want now.

items.title: Why might a representative wait for a CRA clearance certificate before distributing anything?
items.detail: It shows the tax is paid, so they won’t have to pay it out of their own pocket later.

sections.title: Your Action: Build an Estate Readiness Inventory

blocks.text: Don’t change any legal documents or beneficiary forms for this exercise. Just collect the facts first. This is preparation, not legal, tax or financial advice.
This is a fact-finding pass, not a legal filing. Leave passwords, full account numbers, your SIN and copies of legal documents out of this form.

items.title: Administrator
items.text: A person appointed, often by a court, to run an estate when no executor can act.

items.title: Beneficiary
items.text: A person or organization meant to receive money, property or a benefit.

items.title: Clearance certificate
items.text: A CRA letter that says the tax is paid, so the person running the estate isn’t on the hook for it later.

items.title: Estate
items.text: The property, rights, debts and duties left to deal with after a person dies.

items.title: Executor
items.text: A person named in a will to run an estate. Other places may say estate trustee, personal representative or liquidator.

items.title: Intestate
items.text: Dying without a valid will that covers the property.

items.title: Liquidator
items.text: The usual term in Quebec for the person who settles an estate.

items.title: Power of attorney
items.text: A legal document that lets someone act for you in set matters while you’re alive.

items.title: Probate
items.text: A court process that confirms someone’s authority to run an estate or confirms a will. Names and steps vary.

items.title: Successor holder
items.text: Where allowed, a spouse or common-law partner named to take over a TFSA after the holder dies.

items.title: Will
items.text: A legal document with instructions for your property and estate after death.
